abstract: Gene drives are commonly modelled as engineered inheritance-biasing systems with fixed performance, showing great potential for controlling disease vectors and other pests. Yet, natural populations contain standing genetic variation potentially capable of modifying drive transmission, resistance allele formation, and drive-associated fitness. This could lead to evolution in the population after the release of a drive system, potentially affecting the outcome. Here we use individual-based panmictic and spatial mosquito models to examine how standing genetic variation responds to the release of a homing drive configured for population suppression. Genetic variation affecting drive conversion efficiency showed a robust anti-drive response, evolving towards reduced conversion and resulting in inferior outcomes if rapid population elimination was avoided. In contrast, variation affecting embryo resistance and drive fitness cost showed context-dependent evolutionary responses associated with the spatial dynamics of the drive. These could evolve to either increase and inhibit the drive or decrease and improve drive outcomes. Evolving genetic variation in dispersal slightly increased successful elimination outcomes. Recessive deleterious variation acting through inbreeding depression reduced the minimum post-release population size, potentially increasing population elimination rates. However, its effects were not effective in the long-term since deleterious mutations were quickly purged among populations that persisted. Together, these results identify component and scenario-specific evolutionary trajectories based on drive pressure and available standing genetic variation. Thus, standing genetic variation may be treated as a dynamic part of theoretical gene drive modeling and could be worth experimentally quantifying for some possible release candidates.
